chunks.heading: Chapter 9 353
chunks.content:
controls. Additionally, there is often a misunderstanding of what proper token validation looks like.
Figure 9.16 shows the different access control mechanisms that must be validated:

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 355
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 355
Figure 9.16 – Access control mechanisms
First and foremost, it’s important to understand that the structure and content of an access token
can vary depending on the authorization flow used to obtain it. An access token issued on behalf
of a user typically includes more claims than one obtained via the Client Credentials flow, which
represents an application-only context. Regardless of the flow or token format, certain elements
must always be validated systematically:
• The signature: The authorization server signs the token using its private key. To ensure its
authenticity, you must validate the signature using the corresponding public key, which
can be retrieved from the URL specified in the jwks_uri attribute found in the OIDC well-
known metadata endpoint. Relying solely on the token’s payload without verifying its
signature poses a serious security risk.
• The issuer: The iss claim represents the issuer. Checking this ensures the token was
generated by a trusted issuer.
Security Architecture 356
• The audience: The aud claim represents the audience(s), meaning the identifier of the
resource server(s). With this, you are sure that the client effectively requested a token to
talk to you.
• The expiration date: The exp claim represents the expiration date and time of the token.
Checking this ensures you do not let stale tokens go through.
• The not before claim: The nbf claim should ideally be verified as it represents the time
from which backends can process it.
It may also be useful to check the appid claim, which represents the identifier of the client appli -
cation used by the business service, if you want to restrict a backend to a given caller or a limited
set of callers. This can be particularly useful in server-to-server scenarios.
Beyond the basic validations, roles and scopes can also be leveraged—though they fulfill en -
tirely distinct functions. RBAC is applied by inspecting the role claim, which may include one
or more entries representing the roles defined by the resource server. These roles are injected
by Entra ID, either statically according to the client application’s registration or through user or
group assignments to the resource server’s application object, which links specific user groups
to designated roles.
For more advanced scenarios, RBAC might not be sufficient, and Attribute-Based Access Control
(ABAC) should be used instead. ABAC determines access based on a combination of attributes
that reflect business rules. ABAC often requires Claims Augmentation to inject additional claims
next to the default ones. For example, ABAC might be useful with rules such as this: Allow access
if the user is a French subscriber and has a gold-level subscription.
Next in line is the scope claim, which is often a source of confusion in OAuth 2.0. Many develop -

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 355
chunks.content:
ers tend to rely on scopes without deeper scrutiny—simply verifying their presence in a token to
allow API access. However, scopes should be treated as tools to define the boundaries of your APIs.
They enable the authorization server to clearly communicate to users that a client application
seeks to access specific features of a resource server on their behalf. This facilitates an informed
consent experience, empowering users to either approve or reject the requested access. A user
might have consented to the requested access, but it doesn’t mean the user actually has that
permission over the resource server. Here is a concrete example to clarify further: a marketplace
application may request the Microsoft Graph Sites.ReadWrite.All delegated permission, and
the user might consent to it, but the business service using the app should still be restricted to
the site collections the user has access to. In this case, SharePoint Online (the resource server)
validates the actual access of the user for which the token was requested and does not blindly
trust the Sites.ReadWrite.All scope injected by Entra ID in the token. The same considerations
apply to your own APIs.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 357
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 357
That concludes our coverage of OIDC—now, let’s turn our attention to Privileged Access Man -
agement (PAM)and Enterprise Access Management (EAM).
Introducing PAM and red tenant architectures
PAM is a cybersecurity strategy and set of technologies designed to control, monitor, and secure
access to critical systems.
PAM helps minimize the risk of security breaches by enforcing the principle of least privilege,
providing just-in-time and just-enough access, auditing privileged actions, and isolating cre -
dentials in secure vaults.
At this stage, the Microsoft ecosystem provides a vaultless PAM model as there is no integrated
credential vault with password rotation and session isolation, which is why third parties such as
CyberArk and Thycotic are often used in addition to the Microsoft stack. Talking about these is
beyond the scope of this book, but be aware that they are the usual suspects in many companies.
Every serious organization has a PAM strategy that belongs to the broader Identity and Gover -
nance Administration (IGA) concept. However, the extent to which you implement a full-fledged
IGA or PAM, or something more basic, often depends on the industry and your risk appetite.
Implementing IGA is crucial for strengthening security, supporting regulatory compliance, and
boosting operational efficiency.
The core features of Entra ID’s IGA, made available by the Entra Suite plan, include user onboard -
ing and offboarding, policy-driven permission assignments through entitlement management,
and effective recertification via access reviews. Together, these capabilities strengthen the overall
PAM approach.
Now, let’s explore Enhanced Security Admin Environment (ESAE) and Enterprise Access Model
(EAM), which are PAM-friendly architectures.
Microsoft introduced the concept of red forest about a decade ago, which targeted Active Directory
and mostly focused on on-premises environments. Red forest is part of the ESAE practice. The
red forest concept relies on the following tiers:
• Tier 0: This tier represents the crown jewels of your identity assets. Systems such as Active
Directory Domain Services (AD DS), Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), AD FS, Privileged
Access Workstation (PAW), and highly privileged accounts (for example, domain admin),
are part of Tier 0. In the red forest architecture, this tier is fully managed by a separate
Active Directory. Administrators receive PAWs to perform their administrative work and
use another regular device for non-administrative work, such as writing docs and col -
laborating with others.
Security Architecture 358
• Tier 1: This tier includes member servers (application servers, SQL servers, and so on),
as well as the server admin accounts. It basically includes all the servers except those
belonging to tier 0.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 357
chunks.content:
• Tier 2: This tier includes user workstations and help desk support tools, as well as ac -
counts needed to manage tier 2 assets. Tier 2 accounts cannot access tier 1 or tier 0 assets.
While ESAE is now considered legacy—though still in use—it has been succeeded by EAM, which
has become the standard for modern and cloud-native environments since around 2020. EAM
builds on some of ESAE’s foundational principles, such as the tiered architecture, but redefines
the tiers based on logical boundaries such as the control plane (former tier 0), management
plane, and data/workload plane (former tier 1), as well as user access and app access (former tier
2). Despite the shift in structure, EAM shares the same objective as ESAE: to uphold the principle
of least privilege and enforce strong governance over all high-privilege activities. Another key
distinction between EAM and ESAE is that in EAM, high-privilege admin accounts reside strictly
within the control plane, and the zero-trust security model is strictly enforced using CAPs.
While EAM is not prescriptive about using a single- or multi-tenant approach, an emerging trend
consists of using a separate red tenant to control and manage all control plane assets. Red tenant
admin users leverage Entra ID’s cross-tenant access capabilities to gain access to the blue tenant
(workforce/resource tenant), where roles are effectively granted. Using separate tenants enforces
stronger isolation between the control plane and the other layers, as well as dependencies. For
example, the Intune admin in the workforce tenant only exists in that tenant, and as such is fully
isolated from the red tenant. It also allows us to make sure PAWs can only be used by red tenant
users, and the workforce tenant would block any office user using regular machines to perform
administration tasks using CAPs. Admin users typically log in to PAWs using strong authentica -
tion mechanisms, such as FIDO2 keys, and receive their privileges (just in time and just enough)
through a PIM session.
Figure 9.17 illustrates what EAM may look like using a red tenant:

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 359
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 359
Figure 9.17 – Example of what EAM with red tenant may look like
It is important to understand that there is no definitive rule for determining which service be -
longs to which layer. Figure 9.17 illustrates a sample set of Azure services categorized under the
workload/data plane; however, this is by no means exhaustive. As a general guideline, any service
that hosts data or runs workloads is considered part of the workload/data plane. Services that
support the operation and administration of the environment fall under the management plane.
Components enabling user and application access are part of the user and app access layer. The
red tenant is strictly limited to core identity services and is responsible for managing highly
privileged accounts.
Security Architecture 360
However, as is often the case, putting theory into practice can be challenging. In Figure 9.17, a clear
tension emerges: Microsoft Intune is included in the red tenant to manage and enforce controls
on PAWs. While Intune is theoretically part of the management plane, the red tenant is intended
to be strictly limited to control plane assets. This represents a necessary deviation from the mod -
el, as PAWs cannot reasonably be managed by an Intune instance residing in a different tenant.
While the use of PAWs enhances security, it can be seen as a logistical and financial burden—par -
ticularly at scale—since it often involves provisioning and managing multiple physical devices per
administrator. It also means that administrators may need to carry two separate devices when
commuting, which can be inconvenient.
As a potential alternative—albeit with a lower security posture—a Virtual Privileged Access
Workstation (VPAW) restricted to red tenant users only and hosted on Azure Virtual Desktop
can serve as a more flexible solution.
The company glueckkanja has an Azure Marketplace product called Managed Red Tenant that
is moving in that direction, which may be worth evaluating depending on your organization’s
needs and risk tolerance.
For additional information on PAM, you can read some of the online documentation: https://
learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/privileged-access-workstations/privileged-
access-access-model.
Zooming in on CSPM
CSPM is a proactive approach that consists of continuously assessing the security posture of an
environment. CSPM ensures the overall configuration adheres to the best security practices. Any
deviation is flagged, and recommendations are made to remediate non-compliant resources.
Figure 9.18 shows the different built-in tools that help ensure a proper security posture in Azure:

This policy essentially verifies whether the Microsoft.Sql/servers/publicNetworkAccess prop -
erty is set to Disabled. If it’s not, the policy enforces compliance by setting it to Disabled using
the Modify effect. While this approach is practical—since it automatically corrects non-compliant
configurations rather than blocking them—it can conflict with stateful infrastructure-as-code
or GitOps-based tools such as Terraform or Argo CD, potentially leading to deployment issues
later on. If you’re using such tools, it’s recommended to use the Deny effect instead. This ensures
that deployments are compliant from the outset, avoiding hidden drifts and conflicts caused by
automatic modifications. The rule engine is very powerful and allows you to evaluate nearly any
resource attribute. Azure has hundreds of built-in policies and lets you build your own.
Beyond just controlling deployments, policies continuously assess the entire environment and
provide insights, as well as tools such as remediation tasks to restore compliance.
You can visit this link to find hundreds of policy examples: https://github.com/Azure/azure-
policy.
Exploring Foundational and Defender CSPM plans
The Foundational CSPM (free tier) is a multi-cloud solution that adds a layer of intelligence,
visibility, and context on top of Azure Policy. It comes with features such as the secure score and
actionable recommendations about what you should do to fix some security issues. Figure 9.19
shows the secure score that is calculated by Foundational CSPM:
Figure 9.19 – Secure score in Foundational CSPM
Foundational CSPM provides many recommendations of different types. Figure 9.20 shows rec -
ommendations related to storage accounts:

When you click on a specific recommendation, you’re either given the option to fix it immediately
or provided with guidance on how to resolve the issue.
Figure 9.21 – CSPM remediation example
While it might be tempting to click the Fix button, you should always assess the cost impact
before doing so. Moreover, this could conflict with your infrastructure-as-code practice, so you
should include the fix in the next infrastructure-as-code release.
You may encounter hundreds of recommendations, depending on the overall state of your envi -
ronment. However, Foundational CSPM does not evaluate risk factors or the possible attack paths
since it is only made available by Defender CSPM.
Defender CSPM essentially identifies possible attack paths and maps them to the MITRE ATT&CK
framework, a well-known classification of cyberattacks and intrusions. There is a significant
difference between the two plans, and you can evaluate them in detail by reviewing the informa -
tion available at this link: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/

One interesting feature, among others, that is part of Defender CSPM is Microsoft Defender Ex -
ternal Attack Surface Management (EASM).
It’s a specialized offering designed to assess all your existing externally facing assets. It scans
your domains, certificates, and open ports, then provides a detailed report with findings and
actionable recommendations for remediation. It also provides visibility into assets you may have
overlooked or forgotten to decommission, helping reduce unnecessary exposure and optimize
resource management.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 365
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 365
Finally, another notable capability is Defender for DevOps, which is part of Defender CSPM. It
connects your Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) tools to Azure, providing a unified view
for end-to-end CSPM visibility and oversight across your development and deployment processes.
Zooming in on CWPP
CSPM and CWPP are closely related, but the key distinction lies in their focus: CSPM takes a
proactive approach by continuously evaluating security posture and configurations to prevent
attacks, whereas CWPP focuses on threat detection at runtime.
In Azure, Microsoft Defender for Cloud is the cornerstone of CWPP, along with other Defender
options. Figure 9.22 shows the most commonly used options:
Figure 9.22 – CWPP most common options
Figure 9.22 illustrates the granularity of Defender, allowing you to enable all features or selectively
activate only those deemed most critical. Billing is generally based on the specific plans enabled
and the number of protected resources.
Security Architecture 366
All Defender variants integrate directly with Microsoft XDR or Sentinel—tools used to support
SecOps activities, which we will cover later in this chapter. In addition, most Defender offerings
also contribute to CSPM by providing proactive recommendations to further harden the protected
services. Defender sends both signals and security alerts to XDR or Sentinel, which are used to
analyze and respond to security incidents.
Microsoft Defender for Identity primarily covers Active Directory and AD FS to identify and detect
threats against these on-premises infrastructures.
Defender for Resource Manager focuses on interactions with the Azure Resource Manager (ARM)
API, which includes any action performed with the Azure portal, the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell,
and infrastructure as code. It can detect anomalies such as impossible travel (for example, an
action from the US at 9 a.m. followed by another from France an hour later), the use of exploit
toolkits, and malicious virtual machine extensions.
Defender for Databases is centered around SQL Server (all forms: Azure SQL, SQL Managed In -
stance, and self-hosted SQL servers), Cosmos DB, as well as other relational database engines. It
protects against SQL injections, access from unusual data centers, brute-force attacks, and so on.
Defender for APIs is particularly valuable given the central role of APIs in modern architectures.
It detects anomalies such as unusual spikes in API usage or irregular payload sizes by comparing
them to baseline traffic patterns. It also checks whether the API endpoints are subject to authori -
zation. Additionally, it can classify the types of data handled by your APIs, helping you understand
what is exposed to consumers.
Defender for AI helps protect against prompt injections, wallet attacks, and the exposure of sensi -

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 365
chunks.content:
tive data to LLMs, among other things. Wallet attacks, in particular, can be mitigated using the AI
Gateway pattern discussed in Chapter 8, Artificial Intelligence Architecture . Enabling Defender for
APIs on an API that shields the LLM using the AI Gateway pattern can be effective, not because of
Defender’s features themselves, but because the LLM stays hidden while the proxy API is protected.
Both Defender for Storage and Defender for Endpoint offer malware protection, but Defender for
Endpoint provides much broader coverage for virtual machines, with the ability to detect a wide
range of threats occurring within those environments. Needless to say that Defender for Storage is
particularly interesting when using Azure Storage’s SFTP feature. Blobs are tagged once scanned,
and the scan results can be captured using Event Grid for further actions. Note that at this stage,
Defender for Storage does not use sandboxing, which is a way to execute suspicious files into an
isolated environment, enabling advanced threat protection.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 367
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 367
Defender for Containers protects against reconnaissance activities, lateral movements, and cryp -
to-mining, among other things. Additionally, Defender for Containers performs container image
scanning, including daily re-scans. Microsoft has written a simulation script that generates at -
tacks from within an AKS cluster. The script is available here: https://raw.githubusercontent.
com/microsoft/Defender-for-Cloud-Attack-Simulation/refs/heads/main/simulation.py.
Defender for DNS should move to Defender for Servers with the same protection coverage. It
protects against communication with malicious DNS resolvers and malicious domains, anom -
alous protocols, and network patterns. A threat that Defender for DNS cannot detect on its own
is the so-called dangling DNS, which occurs when a malicious party takes over a subdomain. In
short, if you have a web app hosted at a subdomain such as contoso.azurewebsites.net and
a corresponding CNAME record in your DNS, deleting the app without removing the CNAME
leaves a vulnerability. A malicious actor could register a new App Service with the same sub -
domain, effectively hijacking your DNS entry, which makes you lose control over the content of
the subdomain. Defender for App Service helps mitigate as it includes dangling DNS detection.
Although using Azure Firewall as a DNS proxy isn’t strictly part of workload protection, it remains
a valuable complementary approach for routing DNS traffic through Azure Firewall.
Given the fast-paced evolution of the Defender ecosystem, it’s important to regularly reassess its
capabilities when defining and implementing a CWPP strategy.
You can visit the following link for a comprehensive view of the security alerts generated by the
various Defender options: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/
alerts-reference.
It’s worth noting that investing in CSPM is far more effective than relying solely on CWPP. CSPM
takes a proactive approach by continuously verifying that security best practices are enforced
across your environments, helping to prevent cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities. CWPP
serves as a complementary layer, but it should not be your only line of defense.
Zooming in on DevSecOps
Because CI/CD was already introduced in Chapter 2, Solution Architecture, this section will focus
exclusively on security practices.
The purpose of DevSecOps is to integrate security practices into the DevOps or GitOps process. It
is based on the shift-left principle, which consists of shifting some responsibilities to development
teams and making sure to tackle security concerns as early as possible in the development life cycle.
Security Architecture 368
DevOps and GitOps both heavily rely on automation. As mentioned in the introduction, security
teams often operate in silos, with approval processes relying on tickets and occurring outside the

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 367
chunks.content:
DevOps pipeline. The core objective of DevSecOps is to break down these barriers by embedding
security checks and approvals directly into the automation workflow.
The most effective way to achieve this is by involving security analysts directly in the CI/CD
approval process. This means having them participate in peer reviews and approve or reject
security-related changes through pull requests. To streamline this workflow, quality gates can
be established to ensure that no solution is promoted to higher environments until it meets the
required security and compliance standards.
Figure 9.23 shows different tools and DevSecOps practices that should be enforced in any orga -
nization:
Figure 9.23 – DevSecOps
The shift-left principle involves conducting early security checks in the development life cycle,
primarily through Software Composition Analysis (SCA) and SAST. Both techniques analyze
source code to detect potential vulnerabilities and provide remediation guidance. These scans
are typically integrated into build pipelines to catch issues before deployment. They generate
reports that typically include severity ratings or risk levels that can be used to define quality gates.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 369
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 369
In practice, these reports are often overlooked unless strict quality gates are enforced. Apart from
tools like PSRules that scan IaC artefacts, Azure does not provide native SAST or SCA frameworks.
Third-party tools such as Snyk and AppScan can be integrated to fill this gap. Snyk, in particular,
offers strong capabilities for scanning container images—an essential complement to source
code analysis to ensure end-to-end security.
Once the code is built and meets the required quality standards, it should be deployed. Ideally,
DAST tools and a strong CSPM solution should be integrated from the development environment
onward. This enables early detection of runtime vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, reinforcing
security throughout the application life cycle. As we have seen in the Zooming in on CSPM sec -
tion, only Azure Policy and the Foundational plan of Defender are already impressive from that
perspective. For AKS-hosted workloads, policies are defined in Azure Policy and enforced by the
Gatekeeper admission controller, ensuring deployments are compliant with security best practices.
For those willing to go the extra mile, enabling runtime protection from the development envi -
ronment provides enhanced visibility into potential live threats as workloads run. In the Azure
ecosystem, this can be achieved through Defender for Cloud workload protection, with Defender
for Containers offering specialized coverage for containerized environments, as we have seen
in our Zooming in on CWPP section. An alternative, though not mutually exclusive, is to rely on
Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) to further strengthen the security level of appli -
cations through context-aware agents, but this practice is not common and is often overkill if all
the other tools mentioned in this section are already in use.
Lastly, Defender for DevOps is yet another option that lets you plug Defender into your SDLC
solutions (GitHub and Azure DevOps for now). Once onboarded, Defender will scan both the
infrastructure code and the entire repositories and pipelines, providing not only code recom -
mendations but also insights for the DevOps environments themselves.
Let’s now look at security operations, also known as SecOps.
Zooming in on SecOps
At the very end of the application life cycle comes SecOps, which is a practice aimed at detecting,
responding to, and mitigating security threats. The primary purpose of SecOps is to continuous -
ly monitor the live environment. We leverage CSPM upstream as a way to proactively prevent
misconfigurations and vulnerabilities, and CWPP and SecOps downstream to monitor the live
environment, as well as to generate and handle security incidents.
Security Architecture 370
Figure 9.24 depicts the SecOps landscape in Azure:

Figure 9.24 – SecOps landscape in Azure
Extended Detection and Response (XDR) is ensured by Microsoft XDR, a unified solution that
correlates signals coming from all the Defender products. Its portal is the one-stop shop for every
SecOps team member, as it also integrates Azure Sentinel.
However, Sentinel is still considered a SIEM/SOAR solution, used to connect various data sources
to ingest log data and receive security incidents generated by Defender. The logical sequence to
ingest and work with data in Sentinel is shown in Figure 9.25.
Figure 9.25 – Sentinel configuration sequence
Once you install a provider using Content Hub, you can configure its corresponding data connec -
tor(s) to ingest the data you want to retrieve. Each provider comes with a default set of analytic
rules and playbooks, which help you analyze and react to ingested data.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 371
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 371
There are two types of rules, both written in KQL: scheduled and Near-Real-Time (NRT). NRT
rules provide up-to-the-minute threat detection but are currently limited to 50 per customer,
which means that you should carefully select rules for which you consider an immediate detec -
tion and response should be given.
Data is ingested into Log Analytics, and it is considered best practice to work with a dedicated
workspace for Sentinel.
The volume of ingested data can be substantial, potentially resulting in high ingestion costs. It’s
important to carefully choose only the data sources that are truly relevant to your environment.
Additionally, consider setting a daily cap on the Log Analytics workspace to avoid unexpected
cost overruns—especially in non-production environments.
One of the key data sources commonly integrated with Microsoft Sentinel is Entra ID. It provides
valuable insights to detect credential-based attacks such as password spraying and credential
stuffing, as well as anomalies in credential usage. To fully benefit from this data source, you must
have at least a P1 or P2 Entra ID license.
Another essential data source when using virtual machines (IaaS) is Defender for Servers, espe -
cially when combined with Defender for Endpoint and other virtual machine-specific protection
mechanisms. Since the attack surface of virtual machines is typically broader than that of PaaS
services, it’s crucial to enable these Defender solutions and ingest their data and alerts into Sen -
tinel to gain a comprehensive view of your infrastructure’s security posture.
Responding to incidents involves automation rules that allow the automatic assignment of an
owner, a tag, a severity, and to respond with concrete actions using playbooks.
Playbooks are based on Logic Apps workflows, which give you all the flexibility in terms of how
you want to handle and respond to an incident.
The challenge with Sentinel is finding the right balance between noise—too many false positives—
and silence—actual threats not being detected and handled. Setting up Sentinel and connecting
data sources can be done in minutes, but the actual work resides in the setup of analytical rules and
playbooks. Additionally, SecOps team members should connect to the XDR portal on a daily basis.
Third-party solutions such as Splunk and QRadar are also commonly used in SOAR/SIEM and
broader SecOps scenarios. In such cases, they are typically integrated with Azure Event Hubs to
ingest logs and perform detection and response activities accordingly.
Security Architecture 372
Zooming in on appliances and CASB solutions
Figure 9.26 shows the common technologies used as appliances and CASB solutions in Azure:
Figure 9.26 – Appliances and CASB solutions
We previously introduced the concepts of WAFs and next-generation firewalls in Chapter 3, In -

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 371
chunks.content:
frastructure Design, without exploring them in depth. In this section, we’ll delve into Azure WAF
policies and Azure Firewall. It is important to note that many organizations opt for third-party
solutions—such as F5, Imperva, or Cloudflare for WAF capabilities, and Palo Alto, Fortinet, or
Check Point for firewalls. A layered approach is also common, for example, using Cloudflare as
the global entry point and Application Gateway with WAF policies as a secondary WAF, offering
an additional layer of protection. Let’s further explore WAF policies.
Diving deeper into WAF policies
Azure WAF policies consist of both managed rules and custom rules. These policies can be asso -
ciated with either Azure Front Door (serving as a global WAF) or Application Gateway (acting as
a regional WAF). Each policy can operate in either prevention mode, where malicious requests
are blocked, or detection mode, where traffic is monitored but not actively blocked.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 373
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 373
A recommended best practice is to enable WAF policies in detection mode early in the development
life cycle. This allows teams to review WAF logs, identify potential policy violations, and provide
actionable feedback to development teams. However, in practice, WAF logs are often overlooked,
which can result in unexpected disruptions when switching to prevention mode—potentially
causing applications to malfunction. Continuous monitoring of WAF violations is essential, as
false positives can occur and may lead to legitimate traffic being blocked unnecessarily.
Multiple manage rulesets are available, as shown in Figure 9.27:
Figure 9.27 – Managed rulesets (truncated)
Security Architecture 374
Azure WAF provides two rulesets designed to protect against the well-known Open Worldwide
Application Security Project (OWASP) threats and attacks, along with an additional Micro -
soft-specific ruleset. Each rule can be fully enabled or disabled, and fine-grained exclusions allow
specific parts of a request to be ignored, helping to reduce false positives. A WAF policy can be
associated with different scopes within Application Gateway—globally at the gateway level
(applying to all applications), at the listener level, or per path-based rule. More specific scopes
take precedence over the broader scope. This granularity offers significant flexibility to tailor WAF
policies to the specific needs of each application. You may have a gateway-level policy applying
defaults that you absolutely want to enforce, and more application-specific policies that would ac -
commodate application-specific requirements. WAF policies can also inherit from parent policies.

When enabled in prevention mode, any attempt to perform a malicious request will result in a
403 Forbidden error, as shown by Figure 9.29:

custom rules, such as the one shown in Figure 9.30.

This rule will block any non-Belgium calling client. We can have more advanced rules, including
multiple logical operators.
Security Architecture 376
To see the WAF logs, we must enable a diagnostic setting at the level of Application Gateway (or
Front Door) itself, as shown in Figure 9.31:
Figure 9.31 – Enabling WAF logs
Once enabled, logs will be stored in Log Analytics for further investigation. As highlighted earlier,
you should enable WAF logs in development and have someone looking at the logs. To efficiently
understand them, you may run a KQL query such as this one:
let detectedRequests = AGWFirewallLogs
| where RuleId == "949110"
| project TransactionId, TimeGenerated, ClientIp, RequestUri,
Hostname;
AGWFirewallLogs
| join kind= inner (detectedRequests) on TransactionId
| where RuleId != "949110"
| project TimeGenerated, ClientIp, RequestUri, Hostname, RuleId, Message,
Action, DetailedMessage

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 377
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 377
This will return all transactions for which the anomaly score threshold was reached.
Figure 9.32 – Querying the WAF logs
The rule 949110 appears whenever an anomaly score’s threshold is reached. So, we first get all
the anomalies, and then we join the other log items on the TransactionId attribute. This way,
we have all the events that caused policy violations.
While we generally ask application teams to implement the necessary fixes, this is not always
straightforward, as many violations originate from third-party packages outside their control. In
any case, it is essential to carry out this analysis at an early stage—ideally before switching the
WAF policy to prevention mode. Let’s now look at Azure Firewall.
Diving deeper into Azure Firewall
Azure Firewall was first introduced in Chapter 3, Infrastructure Design, where we also deployed one
as part of our use case. In this section, we will take a deeper dive into Azure Firewall and explore the
key concepts and configurations that are essential to understand when working with this service.
First, it’s important to remember that Azure Firewall is a fully cloud-native service that integrates
seamlessly with the broader Azure ecosystem. It supports full management through infrastruc -
ture as code, offers zone redundancy, and can scale automatically based on CPU usage driven by
network traffic.
Security Architecture 378
Azure Firewall is a stateful service with a built-in Intrusion Detection System (IDS)/ Intrusion Pre-
vention System (IPS) or, in short, IDPS capabilities. It supports the de fi nition of both application
rules (layer 7) and network rules (layer 4), and it allows for the con fi guration of both Destination
Network Address Translation (DNAT) and Source Network Address Translation (SNAT) rules.
Firewall rules are part of a hierarchical structure. Each rule type belongs to a rule collection of a cer-
tain type. Rule collections represent a set of rules and are themselves part of rule collection groups.
Each policy has three default rule collection groups, which are DefaultDnatRuleCollectionGroup,
DefaultNetworkRuleCollectionGroup, and DefaultApplicationRuleCollectionGroup. Firewall
policies can also be linked to a parent policy. All policies can be managed with Firewall Manager.
The rule-processing logic is based on priority numbers, from lowest (highest priority) to highest
(lowest priority) number, but Azure Firewall always fi rst processes DNAT rules, then network
rules, and then application rules. So, you can in fl uence the processing logic by setting your own
priorities, but it will always follow the sequence: DNAT  Network  Application.
Microsoft describes the full logic here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/
rule-processing.
Make sure to get acquainted with this and organize your groups, collections, and rules appropri-

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 377
chunks.content:
ately to make sure the system remains manageable at scale. It is also important to consider the
service limits in terms of how many rules you can have within a rule collection and how many
groups you can have in a policy. Consult this reference for more information: https://learn.
microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/azure-subscription-
service-limits. You should return to this page whenever you design anything in Azure to an-
ticipate possible limits and make sure you design future-proof architectures.
Let’s now explore and test the IDPS and TLS inspection capabilities of Azure Firewall through a
quick use case (you do not need to do it).
We’ll fi rst check the IDPS behavior without TLS inspection. Figure 9.33 illustrates a lab architecture:

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 379
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 379
Figure 9.33 – IDPS use case without TLS inspection
Let’s analyze Figure 9.33:
• Networking: We have two Virtual Networks (VNets), one containing a virtual machine
(source VNet) and the other containing Azure Firewall. We have peered the VNets and
routed all traffic to Azure Firewall.
• Firewall policy rule: Because Azure Firewall denies everything by default, we have added
an overly permissive application rule that allows the source VNet to talk to any destination
using HTTP or HTTPS.
• Firewall policy and firewall configuration: We make sure to enable an IDPS in Alert and
deny mode (at the policy level), and we send all the firewall logs to Log Analytics.
In such a configuration, Azure Firewall will check the source and the destination FQDN and check
whether it’s allowed or not. Because of our overly permissive rule, anything targeting HTTP or
HTTPS from our source VNet is allowed.
Security Architecture 380
An IDPS must be enabled at the level of the firewall policy and has a few modes, as shown in
Figure 9.34:
Figure 9.34 – IDPS mode in Azure Firewall policies
You can choose to completely disable the IDPS, enable it in Alert mode, or use the Alert and deny
mode. When set to Alert mode, the system logs any suspicious activity that matches the IDPS
signature rules. These rules are organized into approximately 39 categories and cover around 16
different protocols. You can easily explore them in the IDPS Signature Rules section of the firewall
policy.
Now that our lab is ready, let’s see the IDPS in action! From our source VNet’s virtual machine,
we attempt to perform a malicious HTTP request and see that it is being blocked by the IDPS.
Figure 9.35 – Malicious HTTP request blocked by the IDPS
DNS resolution works, but curl stays pending forever because it is being blocked by the IDPS.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 381
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 381
Looking at the logs, we can clearly see that the request was captured by the IDPS, as shown in
Figure 9.36:
Figure 9.36 – IDPS alert for our malicious request
We see that this request was categorized as Potentially Bad Traffic and that the description tells
us about a suspicious User-Agent.
This is indeed correct as we specified HaxerMen as User-Agent, which is not standard.
Security Architecture 382
However, running the same query in HTTPS instead of HTTP just goes through, as shown in
Figure 9.37:
Figure 9.37 – Suspicious header not blocked by the IDPS in HTTPS
This behavior is expected due to how the TLS protocol works. In a TLS session, the client (in this
case, the virtual machine in the source VNet) establishes an encrypted tunnel directly with the
destination (for example, google.com). Azure Firewall simply forwards and performs SNAT on
this encrypted traffic. While it can observe limited metadata—such as the target FQDN (such as
google.com)—it cannot inspect the full URL or the contents of the request, including headers or
the body, since they are encrypted. As a result, it cannot detect a malicious header because it has
no visibility into the encrypted payload.
In order to inspect the payload, we need TLS inspection, which is available with Azure Firewall
Premium.
You must enable TLS inspection at the level of the premium firewall policy.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 383
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 383
Figure 9.38 – Enabling TLS inspection in a firewall policy
You must also enable TLS inspection at the level of the application rule. Now, repeating the same
call again with HTTPS, we see that the IDPS kicked in and blocked the request, as with HTTP.
Figure 9.39 – Malicious HTTPS request blocked by the IDPS with TLS inspection enabled
Security Architecture 384
The first call in Figure 9.39 is blocked while the second one goes through. Now, Azure Firewall is
able to inspect the traffic and detect the malicious HTTP header value.
You may have noticed the use of the --insecure flag. For testing purposes, we used the default
Azure Firewall CA certificates without adding the intermediate certificate sent by the firewall
or the root CA to our client machine. As a result, this flag was necessary; otherwise, curl would
have simply failed.
This brings us to a very important aspect of TLS inspection. Although this allows a full inspection
of the HTTP request payload, the price to pay is that all callers must trust the certificates issued
by a private CA. However, this is not always possible as many Azure services do not allow you to
inject a custom CA. Figure 9.40 shows how TLS inspection changed our setup:
Figure 9.40 – How TLS inspection works
With TLS inspection enabled, the firewall is not just forwarding the request but is the actual man
in the middle. There are two HTTP requests going on. The first one is between the source virtual
machine and Azure Firewall, and the second one is between Azure Firewall and the actual destina -
tion. This is why the firewall is able to decrypt the payload. This means that the CA used by Azure
Firewall to issue the intermediate certificates must be trusted on the calling side. For our lab, we
could afford to ignore certificate errors, but this of course would not be possible in a real-world
situation. Moreover, this CA is typically not a public well-known CA, so it is not trusted by default.
A few Azure services allow you to inject custom CAs, such as App Service, hosted in an App Service
Environment (ASE), AKS, and basically any container-based services where you can mount the
CA as a volume. Virtual machines also support the injection of custom CAs.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 385
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 385
Beyond trusting the CA, TLS inspection also has an impact on performance because of the de -
cryption, inspection, and reencryption of the payload. When using a custom firewall, you must
ensure it scales according to the volume of traffic, else it could quickly become a bottleneck,
causing significant latencies.
I strongly advise only enabling TLS inspection for FQDNs that you do not trust or that could lead
to a possible data leakage. I strongly discourage enabling TLS inspection for everything, especially
when targeting services such as Entra ID.
In any case, you should use TLS inspection with care and evaluate the impacts first. To learn more
about Azure Firewall certificates for TLS inspection, you can refer to this online documentation:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/premium-certificates.
CASB solutions in a nutshell
CASB solutions are closely linked to the zero-trust security model, which aims at verifying every
activity happening inside and outside the corporate network, since nothing should be trusted by
default. CASB contributes to zero trust in that it acts as a bridge between users and cloud services,
monitoring which services are accessed, and protecting against threats and data leakage. It is
mostly used on user devices where a CASB client such as Netskope intercepts all traffic destined
for the internet (SaaS solutions, etc.) and performs TLS inspection to prevent possible data leakage
and allow/deny the user device to reach out to the destination.
Microsoft ships with Defender for Cloud Apps, but Netskope and Zscaler are commonly used as
well. Although CASB is initially centered around user traffic, it starts to be more commonly used
for server-side components accessing cloud services.
Zscaler, for example, provides the Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) package as a pure CASB solution
and Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) as a pure zero-trust solution. While not native, they are very
commonly used in large enterprises.
Let’s now summarize this chapter.
Summary
This chapter presented a comprehensive view of security architecture in Azure, emphasizing its
critical role across identity, data, infrastructure, workloads, and operations. It highlighted the
need to modernize security practices through automation, risk-based governance, and closer
alignment between development, operations, and security teams.
Security Architecture 386
Identity was addressed as the new perimeter, with Entra ID providing strong access controls
via Conditional Access, PIM, and support for modern protocols such as OAuth 2.0 and OIDC.
Data security was examined through encryption at rest, in transit, and in use, along with key
management strategies such as BYOK, HYOK, and managed HSM. Governance features such as
Microsoft Purview, audit logs, versioning, and dynamic masking were also discussed to ensure

data integrity. The chapter contrasted CSPM and CWPP, showing how CSPM enables proactive
configuration compliance while CWPP focuses on runtime protection. DevSecOps was reinforced
as a key practice, with integration of SAST, DAST, and container scanning into CI/CD pipelines.
SecOps was covered through Microsoft Sentinel and Defender XDR, using playbooks, analytic
rules, and automation to detect and respond to incidents. The chapter also explored Azure-na -
tive appliances such as Azure Firewall and WAF, including TLS inspection and its operational
implications. Finally, we highlighted the growing use of CASB solutions in the context of zero
trust. Overall, the chapter emphasized that effective cloud security depends on adopting native
capabilities, embracing automation, and aligning security models with the cloud-native paradigm.

valuable resources, including links to further reading and experts to follow, helping you deepen
your understanding and stay updated on emerging trends in the field. This final section ensures

Closing Thoughts and Next
Steps
Writing a book is about making choices. This is especially true when the ambition is to depict the
vast and ever-evolving Azure landscape. Some topics warrant deep technical dives, while others
can only be briefly touched upon, not due to a lack of importance but simply because of scope
and space constraints. Throughout this book, we’ve made deliberate choices to balance depth
with breadth, to provide hands-on insights where possible, and to offer architectural thinking
that resonates with real-world Azure practices. The result is a guided journey through Azure
that equips architects, engineers, and decision-makers with solid knowledge and actionable
insights—without claiming to be exhaustive.
Across the chapters, the book established a logical progression, starting with the fundamentals
of cloud architecture and the diversity of architect roles (Chapter 1). The concept of Azure maps
was introduced early to structure decision-making, enabling readers to navigate Azure services
based on technical intent. Chapter 2 built on this by defining the Solution Architecture Map and
categorizing workloads (for example, SoRs and SoIs), while also introducing maturity models

and governance strategies to manage evolving concerns pragmatically.
The narrative then moved on to core infrastructure and platform services, starting with foundational
practices in networking, monitoring, HA/DR, and security-first designs (Chapter 3). Chapters 4
and 5 zoomed into the container landscape, offering a comprehensive view of AKS—including its
network and security intricacies—and evaluating simpler container alternatives such as Azure
Container Apps and ACI. These chapters helped readers weigh complexity against agility, and
showed how technologies such as Istio and Calico can support multi-tenant SaaS platforms
within AKS.
Closing Thoughts and Next Steps 388
Shifting toward application design, Chapter 6 addressed the cloud development experience, em -
phasizing the importance of the Azure ecosystem when developing solutions. It gave practical
guidance on local development and the must-have skills each developer and application architect
should have.

Chapter 7 broadened the lens to data architectures, dissecting ingestion, storage, and real-time
analytics pipelines. From OLTP stores such as Cosmos DB to OLAP services such as Synapse and
Azure Data Explorer, it painted a layered view of modern data ecosystems. Infrastructure enablers
such as virtual network integration, managed virtual networks, and SHIR were also covered, in -
cluding hybrid scenarios, grounding the discussion in enterprise reality.

chunks.content:
Chapter 8 explored the rise of AI in Azure, contrasting the use of traditional and generative AI. It
introduced vector databases, retrieval-augmented generation, orchestration frameworks, and the
concept of agentic AI, while emphasizing architectural choices around cost, precision, and scal -
ability. We purposely focused on architectural patterns only and avoided any hands-on practical
examples, given the fast-moving pace of the AI realm that would have rendered code samples
obsolete by the time the book reached publication. The aim was to give readers a durable foun -
dation for AI solution design, rather than transient implementation guidance.
Finally, Chapter 9 delivered a holistic view of security architecture, touching on identity, data, work -
loads, and operations. It reinforced the importance of DevSecOps and SecOps practices, explored
the interplay between CSPM and CWPP, and emphasized zero-trust principles through native
Azure capabilities such as Entra ID, Microsoft Purview, Sentinel, and Defender XDR. Automation
and alignment across teams emerged as essential themes, particularly as organizations mature
their cloud security postures.
Altogether, this book is a compass more than an encyclopedia. It provides the maps, the questions,
and the trade-offs—not always the definitive answers. Readers are invited to adapt, extend, and
question its content as they chart their own journey through the Azure cloud.
